content.text:
Yes. I’d use **Entire runners to produce evidence on each trail**, then **gates to decide what must pass before merge**. Entire’s runner setup supports repo-specific prompts in `.entire/runners/*.json`; the installed CLI also exposes trail findings and reviews. [Entire runner reference](https://docs.entire.io/cli-reference/runner.md)

For **girl-dinner**, I’d start with these runners:

| Runner | What it looks for |
|---|---|
| **Security and privacy** | Room-code access, API abuse, photo URL handling, exposed secrets, unnecessary data collection |
| **Correctness** | Broken room and recommendation flows, edge cases, error handling |
| **Confidence** | Whether tests and checks actually cover the changed behavior; missing evidence stated explicitly |
| **Drift** | Changes that conflict with the app’s existing patterns or the trail’s stated goal |
| **Slop** | Generic UI copy, needless abstractions, duplicate code, placeholder behavior, claims the product cannot support |
| **UX and accessibility** | Mobile layout, keyboard use, readable states, loading and error feedback |

I’d make **build/typecheck failures and high-severity security or correctness findings blocking**. Confidence gaps would request review when the affected flow is important. “Slop” should initially be **advisory with specific examples**, since a vague score would be easy to game and frustrating to act on. Every finding should point to a file, behavior, or missing check, and be tied to the trail’s current commit.

This repo already has Entire enabled, but I found **no trail runners configured and no trails listed**. So we could build this as a small pilot: tailor the runners, run them on one real change, tune noisy findings, then turn on the gates that prove useful.
